japanese-jev: A Japanese System One Decision Model on a Laptop GPU# #LLM; #LoRA; #Evaluation; #Calibration; #Japanese
An unofficial reproduction of a “System One” (Jev-style) typed decision model for Japanese. It does not generate text: given a text, a question and a list of options, it returns a probability for each option from a single forward pass.
Repository: https://github.com/bigrh0917/japanese-jev-release · Weights: 1.7B, 0.6B
Not affiliated with TypeSafe AI or Jev.
graph TD A[Public Japanese datasets] --> B[Convert to choice / yes-no / ordinal template] S[1,109 synthetic items: negation, indirect refusals, honorifics] --> C B --> C[LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-1.7B-Base] C --> D[Read option-letter logits at the last position] D --> E[Temperature scaling] E --> F[Evaluation: accuracy, ECE, paired comparisons] F --> G[FastAPI endpoint] Project Overview# Jev is a closed model from TypeSafe AI that answers typed questions (pick one option, yes or no, rate on a scale) with probabilities instead of generated text. Its documentation says accuracy is lower outside English, so I built a small model of the same kind for Japanese to see how far a laptop could get. What Jev is and why it matters is in a separate note: What Is Jev?
The model is Qwen3-1.7B-Base with a LoRA adapter (r=16). Training completions are a single option-letter token; inference reads only those letters’ logits at the last position and applies a softmax, so there is no decoding loop. Everything was trained on one RTX 4060 Laptop GPU (8 GB). A 0.6B version trained with the same recipe is also released.
Goals and Hypotheses# When Jev came out, a common reaction was “this is just a classifier”. If that is true, a 1 to 2B model on a laptop should be able to do it. I wanted to check that, and to see where the method breaks when it is moved to Japanese.
The constraints:
The method is not public. No weights, paper, data or training code. The structure has to be inferred from open reproductions and other people’s black-box probes. 8 GB of GPU memory, one person, about a week. Only models under 2B, and only with LoRA. Japanese data is scarce and restricted. Public classification data is small and comes in different formats. livedoor (CC BY-ND) and WRIME (research only) can be used for evaluation but not for training. Public data has almost no items where the literal and the intended meaning differ. Evaluation is easy to fool. There is no ready-made Japanese evaluation for this kind of model, and accuracy on 500 items carries ±3 to 4 points of error. The first goal was a Japanese model that answers choice, yes/no and ordinal questions, with temperature-calibrated probabilities, behind a /v1/systemone endpoint. After the first round I made it measurable:
Goal Status Pragmatics (self-built set) at 75% or above 69.3%, not reached Ordinal questions clearly above chance on a scale the model has never seen (WRIME) Not reached: 67 on a balanced measure where chance is 50; still the weakest type Numbers on a sealed test set The set exists and has not been run A comparison with Jev itself on the same items Done, 1,600 items A change counts as an improvement only if a paired comparison with the untrained base model at 4-shot gives |z| ≥ 2, and JCommonsenseQA does not drop.
Hypothesis How it was tested Result H1: LoRA on public Japanese data raises accuracy on unseen tasks Paired comparison with the same base at 4-shot No. No unseen set reached |z| ≥ 2 H2: The bottleneck is the lack of pragmatics items in the training data, and targeted synthetic data can fill it Continued training on the first synthetic batch Mostly yes. Pragmatics and negation rose clearly, but the training and test items share an author H3: Learning Jev’s probabilities (distillation) is better than learning the gold answer alone The same 9,510 items, trained once with each objective No. No difference in accuracy, and the change in calibration was inconsistent H4: A broader second synthetic batch, and JCoLA training sentences, keep improving it All three variants trained to the end and compared No. No measurable gain Results# Accuracy (%). “4-shot” is the untrained base model given four examples, which is the fair baseline for what training taught. Jev numbers come from sending the same items to the Jev API (Jev 1.14, through OpenRouter).
Test set Items 0.6B 4-shot 0.6B model 1.7B 4-shot 1.7B model Jev 1.14 Held-out items from the training sources (all three types) 1,000 49.6 77.0 57.9 80.0 – JCommonsenseQA (5-way) 500 67.0 62.4 80.2 81.4 97.0 MASSIVE intents (8-way) 500 75.6 80.0 84.0 86.0 93.4 livedoor news (9 categories) 500 48.0 48.4 50.8 52.4 – WRIME (emotion intensity, ordinal) ¹ 500 50.0 62.2 54.8 67.0 – JCoLA (sentence acceptability, yes/no) ² 500 49.8 52.2 52.6 57.2 – Negation minimal pairs (self-built) 100 69.0 96.0 81.0 97.0 97.0 Pragmatics (self-built, all three types) 300 46.7 61.3 53.0 69.3 89.0 Japanese knowledge (self-built) ³ 200 41.0 42.5 53.0 51.5 84.0 81% of WRIME items are “no emotion”, so always answering the lowest level scores 81% accuracy. This row is the average of “share of no-emotion items answered correctly” and “share of emotion items detected” (50 by chance). Sampled so that natural and unnatural sentences are half and half (50 by chance). The Jev number was measured before the wording of some questions was revised. How to read these:
They are development test sets that I looked at many times while iterating. A sealed set exists but has not been run, and there is one random seed. The margin of error is about ±3 to 4 points at 500 items, ±5.5 at 300 and ±8 at 100. The self-built sets and the synthetic training data share an author (Claude), so those rows are optimistic. On JCommonsenseQA, MASSIVE, livedoor and knowledge, the difference between the trained model and 4-shot is within noise. Training improved negation, pragmatics and emotion intensity, which are the areas the synthetic data covers. MASSIVE here is 8-way (the correct intent plus 7 sampled wrong ones), which is easier than the original 60-way task. The 0.6B model improves on negation and pragmatics too, but on JCommonsenseQA it falls below its own 4-shot baseline (62.4 against 67.0). It is lower than 1.7B on almost every set, by 19 points on JCommonsenseQA. Highlights# Speed: about 25 ms per question locally, roughly 14x faster than having the same model generate a JSON answer (344 ms). An honest baseline: against a 0-shot baseline, training looked like +27 points on JCommonsenseQA; against 4-shot it was +1. On unseen tasks, LoRA on public data alone bought speed and format stability, not accuracy. Targeted data worked: adding 1,109 synthetic items for what public data lacks (negation pairs, indirect refusals, honorific relationships) raised pragmatics from 53 to 69 and negation from 81 to 97. Usable confidence: answering locally only when confidence is at least 0.7 and sending the rest to Jev would skip about 73% of API calls on MASSIVE at 92.2% combined accuracy, against 93.4% for Jev alone. Three Japanese evaluation sets (600 items) for pragmatics, negation and knowledge, released under CC BY 4.0. How the Rebuild Works# Four stages run from one config file, and a server sits on top of the result:
build → data/*.jsonl → train → adapters → calibrate → temperature.json → evaluate → evaluation.json 1. One Template for Three Question Types# Every item, whatever its type, becomes one block of text. The model’s only job is to put the right letter after [decision]:.
[kind] choice [state] 先週注文した商品がまだ届きません。配送状況を教えてください。 [question] この文章の主な目的はどれですか。 [options] A. 依頼: 何かをしてほしいと頼んでいる B. 質問: 情報を尋ねている C. 苦情: 不満を訴えている D. 感謝: お礼を伝えている [decision]: Type Options Shuffled? choice Up to 16 named options, each optionally with a short description Yes noul (yes / no) Always A. yes, B. no No score (ordinal) Levels from lowest to highest No, the order is the scale Training, inference and the API server call the same render() function. The model is very sensitive to this format: one extra space or a missing newline and accuracy drops to chance without any error.
2. Data# Public Japanese datasets are rewritten into the three types, about 55,000 rows in total. All six have licenses that allow training and releasing weights.
Source Becomes License Rows used JNLI choice, 3-way (entailment / contradiction / neutral) CC BY-SA 4.0 Up to the per-type cap, out of 20,000 JSICK noul (does it entail?) and a 5-level score (relatedness) CC BY-SA 4.0 9,000 JSTS 6-level score (similarity) CC BY-SA 4.0 12,451 KUCI choice, 4-way; half the items borrow 4 to 8 wrong options from other items to reach 8 to 12 CC BY-SA 4.0 10,000 PAWS-X (Japanese) noul (same meaning?) Open, with attribution 10,000 MewsC-16 (Japanese) choice, once with all 12 topics and once with a 6-topic subset CC BY 2.5 and others 3,968 The rules that shaped it:
Training and evaluation use different datasets. JCommonsenseQA, MASSIVE, livedoor news, WRIME and JCoLA are evaluation-only, and the build fails if one is listed as a training source. livedoor and WRIME could not be used for training anyway because of their licenses. Duplicates are removed, and when the same item appears with conflicting answers the whole group is dropped. Each question type is capped at 16,000 rows, taken from the sources in turn so that one large dataset does not fill the cap. Choice options are shuffled, and the same source appears with different option sets. The model has to read the option text. It cannot memorize a label set or a position. Many-option items are included on purpose. The first data version had at most five options per item, so the model had never seen the letters after E. Splits are by group. Validation (1,000 rows) and calibration (1,000 rows) are cut from the training pool by source text, so a validation item never has a sibling in the training set. Augmented rows are added at a ratio of 25%: all-hiragana, full-width and half-width variants, an added irrelevant sentence, and permuted options. SIB-200 (7 topics, 1,004 items) is used only in calibration, to fit temperatures. It is neither trained on nor evaluated on. The evaluation sets, which training and calibration never read:
Set Type Items Notes JCommonsenseQA choice, 5-way 500 Same setting other people used to test Jev MASSIVE (Japanese) choice, 8-way 500 Correct intent plus 7 sampled wrong ones livedoor news choice, 9-way 500 Evaluation only (CC BY-ND). Stratified over the 9 categories, site names masked WRIME score, 4 levels 500 Evaluation only (research use). 81% of items are the lowest level JCoLA noul 500 Is the sentence natural? 250 yes, 250 no Pragmatics (self-built) all three 300 17 kinds of pragmatic phenomena: the several meanings of 大丈夫, indirect refusals, double negation, honorifics and relationships, dialect, omitted subjects and others Knowledge (self-built) choice 200 12 kinds of Japanese knowledge Negation (self-built) noul 100 Minimal pairs, 4 sentence patterns × 25 Each evaluation source also has a sealed split that is only to be run once, before reporting numbers.
On top of the public data sit 1,109 synthetic items for things it does not contain, where the literal and the intended meaning differ. They were written by Claude, which is an exception to my own rule of using only open-weight models.
Kind Items Indirect answers 200 Negation minimal pairs (40 verbs × 4 sentence patterns) 160 Emotion intensity 160 Honorifics and relationships 120 Replies to an offer (大丈夫 / 結構 / いい) 119 Negative questions 80 Expressions like 悪くない 60 Idioms 50 How likely a promise is to be kept, certainty, urgency, strength of dissatisfaction 40 each That is 489 choice, 320 score and 300 noul items. Each one is compared with the self-built evaluation items by character 3-gram overlap (Jaccard similarity) and dropped above 0.6. This check was run against the self-built sets only, not the public ones, and it cannot catch sentences that mean the same in different words.
3. Training# Plain supervised fine-tuning with TRL’s SFTTrainer. The loss is computed on the completion only, which is one letter token. Otherwise it is diluted by several hundred prompt tokens and the model learns nothing about the decision.
Setting Value LoRA r=16, alpha=32, dropout 0.05, on q/k/v/o and the gate/up/down projections. PEFT’s default for Qwen3 is q and v only, so the seven modules have to be listed Learning rate 1e-4, cosine schedule, 3% warmup Batch 4 with gradient accumulation 2 (1.7B on 8 GB) Sequence length, precision 512 tokens, bf16, gradient checkpointing Checkpoints Evaluated and saved every 200 steps; the one with the lowest validation loss is kept. Continued training later switched to the last checkpoint Continued training on synthetic data 5e-5: the synthetic items five times over plus 5,000 earlier items to prevent forgetting Distillation variant 0.5 × KL(Jev ‖ student) + 0.5 × cross-entropy on the correct letter, computed over the option letters only Run Model Data Steps and time Smoke test 0.6B A first cut of the public data 1,500 steps, 10 minutes, only to confirm the pipeline works end to end Main training 0.6B and 1.7B About 55,000 rows, group splits 1 epoch for 0.6B, 2 epochs for 1.7B (the longest run, overnight) Continued, first synthetic batch 1.7B and 0.6B Synthetic × 5 + 5,000 earlier items 1,319 steps, about 26 minutes for 1.7B Continued, second and third batches 1.7B and 0.6B First and second batches × 3 each + 6,000 earlier items; the third adds 2,300 JCoLA sentences 1,903 and 2,191 steps, about an hour each for 1.7B Distillation comparison 0.6B 9,510 items 1,189 steps, about 19 minutes each Reading the loss. Because the completion is one token, the loss is the negative log-probability of the correct letter, which makes it easy to interpret. These are rules of thumb for this recipe:
A starting value of 2 to 6 is normal, since the base model does not know it should answer with a letter. It should fall below 1 within the first 100 to 200 steps. A healthy final value is about 0.3 to 0.6. It does not reach 0 because some items are ambiguous. Stuck near ln(K), about 1.4 to 2.1 for 4 to 8 options, means the model is guessing uniformly. That is almost always a template or token mismatch. Validation loss rising while training loss keeps falling is overfitting. Take the checkpoint before the rise. In TRL’s log, loss is the training loss, eval_loss is on the validation set, and mean_token_accuracy is the share of letters answered correctly. The logged loss averages over the letter and the end token, so it is lower than a letter-only loss. A training loss far below the validation loss (0.11 against 0.32 in continued training) means the data has been memorized, usually because a small set was repeated too many times. This is why the later batches were repeated three times, not five. 4. Readout# Inference runs one forward pass and looks at the last position only. The output there is a score for every token in the vocabulary, about 150,000 of them. Of those, only the tokens " A" to " P" matter, and of those only the first n, where n is the number of options in this question. Those n numbers go through a softmax.
Two details decide whether this works at all:
The letter tokens include the leading space. Training writes " A", so the readout must look up the id of " A". Looking up "A" reads a different token and the result is close to random. Long inputs are shortened in the state only. The question, the options and the [decision]: marker must survive intact. Since the letter is only an index into the option list, the same model handles four options or twelve, and the options can change on every request.
5. Calibration# After training the model is over-confident. Temperatures are fitted on the calibration set by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (a one-dimensional search between 0.3 and 6), and the logits are divided by them before the softmax. There is one per question type, and within a type a separate one per option-count bucket (2, 3 to 5, 6 to 16) when the bucket has at least 50 items. The final per-type temperatures are 2.09 (choice), 1.80 (noul) and 1.64 (score).
On the training sources this lowers ECE from 0.114 to 0.043. The same temperatures do not carry over to other datasets: on unseen test sets they sometimes made ECE worse, and fitting on a different dataset (SIB-200) was worse still. So in-distribution results are reported calibrated and out-of-distribution results uncalibrated, and a deployment should refit the temperature on 200 to 500 of its own examples. Changing the calibration set does not need retraining. It is a refit of a few minutes.
6. Evaluation# Accuracy alone is not enough for a model whose product is a probability.
Metric Why Accuracy with a 95% interval 500 items carry about ±3 to 4 points of error Paired comparison on the same items (z; a difference counts at |z| ≥ 2) More reliable than comparing two accuracies ECE (15 bins), Brier, NLL Whether the probabilities can be trusted Automation rate at a 2% or 5% error budget What a business cares about: how much can be handled automatically Permutation consistency Whether the answer survives shuffling the options four times p50 latency Speed is the selling point of this design Balanced accuracy on WRIME Plain accuracy is fooled by always answering the lowest level The controls are the untrained base model at 0-shot and 4-shot, and the Jev API on the same 1,600 items (cost: $0.027). Other people’s reproduction numbers are only an order-of-magnitude reference, since their items and option counts differ.
Checks on the evaluation itself:
Blank the input. Removing the state and keeping only the question and options sends every test set back to chance, so none of them can be answered from the options alone. Intervals and baselines. A script prints confidence intervals, the random and majority-class baselines, paired tests, and a list of suspicious items. Label review. 49 suspicious knowledge items were checked by hand. In three categories where Jev also did badly (counters, kanji readings, correct honorific use), 4 counter items and 6 reading items turned out to be ambiguous or to have a flawed option, and their wording was revised. The item count stayed the same. One ordinal scale (how likely a promise is to be kept) was not mislabeled but too fine: one sentence cannot separate “almost none” from “low”. Speed re-measured after finding that earlier latencies were taken with GPU memory filled by my own code. Comparing with the Jev API fairly:
My type What is sent to Jev What comes back choice criteria as option name → description The selected option and a probability per option noul instructions as the question The probability of “yes” score criteria as the ordered list of levels A score and a probability per level The highest-probability option is taken as the answer and stored in the same prediction format as my own model, so the same script does the paired comparison. Accuracy, ECE and automation rate can be compared, because the items and options are identical. Latency cannot, because one side includes a network round trip. Items whose licenses do not allow it (WRIME, livedoor) and the sealed set were not sent. Jev scored 97.0 on JCommonsenseQA, close to the 97.8 someone else reported, which suggests the hookup is right.
Ablations: 0.6B against 1.7B; 0-shot, 4-shot and LoRA; distillation with and without Jev’s probabilities; the three synthetic batches (the third against the second is a clean comparison, differing only in JCoLA); LoRA merged against unmerged.
7. Serving and Speed# A small FastAPI server exposes /v1/systemone with the same request and response shape as Jev’s API: one state, several typed questions, probabilities and a confidence back. Each question is rendered to its own prompt and gets its own forward pass.
Setting Per question 1.7B, one question at a time (LoRA merged) 25 ms 1.7B, batches of 8 12 ms Untrained base model + 4 examples 94 ms Same model generating a JSON answer (15 tokens) 344 ms Jev API, one question at a time (from Japan, including network) 377 ms Measured on JCommonsenseQA, 200 items × 3 rounds, on the RTX 4060 Laptop GPU. Most of Jev’s 377 ms is network time, and Jev can answer several questions in one request, so this is not a comparison of model speed. What it shows is that running locally removes the round trip, and that reading probabilities is an order of magnitude faster than generating an answer.
Other measurements on the 1.7B model:
Permutation consistency. The share of items answered the same way after shuffling the options went from 0.69 to 0.93 with training. Robustness. Rewriting the input in all hiragana costs 13 to 47 points. Adding an irrelevant sentence at the end stays within ±3 points on every set. Over-confidence. Trained to the end, the temperatures are 1.6 to 2.1, so the raw probabilities must be recalibrated before use. Implementation Details That Mattered# Compute logits for the last position only. The first version produced vocabulary-sized logits for every position, which filled the 8 GB of memory and more than doubled every latency I had measured. Fixing it is what brought a question down to 25 ms. Merge the LoRA weights before serving. Unmerged is about 75% slower (44 ms against 25 ms). Resume from checkpoints. Laptop sleep stalled one overnight run and an automatic Windows update killed another. Check the data after every build: answer distribution, whether options were shuffled, and whether any evaluation text leaked into training. Three rules that cannot be bent:
The text format in training and in inference must be identical. The model learns that at the end of text in this exact format the next token is the answer letter. Any difference (one more space, one fewer newline, a letter with or without its leading space) and accuracy falls to chance, with no error. When an input is too long, shorten the state only. The model answers at the position after the option list and the decision marker. Shorten the state to fit the budget before assembling the text; do not cut the assembled text from the end. Training, calibration and evaluation sets do not overlap, and each has one job. Training updates the weights. Calibration only fits the temperature. Evaluation only produces the final numbers and never changes, so versions stay comparable. The order I worked in: one item all the way through first, checking the assembled text, the token ids and the logits at the last position. Then a few training steps, to confirm the loss falls and the saved weights load. Then the full run.
Timeline# Date Work Nov 7 Read up on Jev and the open reproductions Nov 8 Environment, data conversion, first 0.6B run Nov 9–10 Many-option data, switch to 1.7B, self-built pragmatics and knowledge sets Nov 11 Audit: three of the good numbers turned out to be artifacts; fixed the test sets and splits Nov 12–13 Second round with the 4-shot control and negation set; clean speed test; synthetic data; Jev comparison; distillation; routing estimate Nov 14 More synthetic variants; found the checkpoint-selection problem; fixed the final model Nov 15 Release: code, weights, evaluation sets, comparison numbers Key Decisions# Decision Why Alternatives considered Trade-off Read the option letters’ logits, with no extra decision head Trains with little data; standard SFT tools and no change to the model; close to what Jev is thought to be A pointer head (about a million parameters trained from scratch, needs more data); an encoder with a marker scoring head (Chinese-Jev used about ten million items) At most 16 options; letters carry a prior, which has to be held down by shuffling and checked with permutation consistency Qwen3 Base; get 0.6B working, then move to 1.7B The Base version has no chat template, which suits reading logits; 1.7B is 19 points ahead of 0.6B on JCommonsenseQA Qwen3.5-0.8B (needs an extra library on CUDA); anything larger (does not fit in 8 GB) 1.7B only trains at batch 4 with gradient accumulation 2 Change the control from 0-shot to 4-shot A 0-shot base model does not even know the answer format, so any training looks like a large gain Report 0-shot only, as I did at first The “gain” from training went from about 27 points to not significant. The conclusion looks worse and is true Paired tests, not just accuracy differences 500 items carry ±3 to 4 points, so small differences cannot be read Compare accuracies Many “improvements” are judged not significant Synthetic data written by Claude Time was short and local generation was not good enough Generate with an open-weight model; write by hand Training and test items share an author, so scores are optimistic. Marked as an exception Continue training on the existing LoRA, not from scratch 26 minutes against several hours Train from scratch Old tasks can be forgotten, so 5,000 earlier items are mixed in Use the Jev API as a distillation teacher A ready-made, calibrated teacher at very low cost ($0.19 for 9,510 items) A large open-weight model as teacher A second exception to the open-weight rule. The teacher’s labels and the distilled weights are not part of the release. The labeling script resumes where it stopped and has a spending cap Stop distillation at 9,510 items, and do not run it on 1.7B The small experiment already showed no difference, so labeling the remaining 48,000 items was not worth paying for Label everything, then compare The conclusion holds only for 0.6B, one seed, and this one way of using a teacher Do not claim it is faster than Jev Most of the 377 ms is network, and Jev answers several questions per request “About 10x faster than the Jev API”, from an early draft A weaker pitch, but every sentence can be checked Report in-distribution results calibrated and out-of-distribution results uncalibrated Temperatures measurably do not transfer across datasets One temperature for every set Out-of-distribution ECE cannot be made to look good; the deployer has to refit Balanced accuracy for WRIME 81% of items are the lowest level, so “always lowest” scores 81% Keep reporting accuracy Cannot be compared with other people’s accuracy Keep both base models fixed Get the data and evaluation solid first; the four-column comparison (two sizes, before and after training) stays comparable Qwen3.5, or a Japanese-specific base “Would a different base fix the knowledge questions?” stays unanswered Synthetic data must be broad and not aimed at known test items Patching the test set’s errors raises the score by practicing the test Target the errors The second batch showed no effect on the existing sets JCoLA training sentences as a separate third batch Only a separate run shows what caused a change Mix them into the second batch No public yes/no evaluation set is left that the model has never practiced When a self-built item has a problem, only reword the question Options and labels stay, the item count stays, and the original label holds Delete the item or change options Scores before and after the rewording cannot be compared directly Send only some items to the third-party API The WRIME and livedoor licenses do not allow it, and the sealed set must stay unseen Send everything Jev has no numbers on those sets A fresh directory for the public repository No development history, no working comments, code and output in English Make the working repository public Two directories to maintain Release both sizes 0.6B is lighter, 1.7B is more accurate; the user chooses Release 1.7B only The 0.6B weights had to be moved over from the training machine Smaller calls: run 0.6B for 1,500 steps to confirm the whole pipeline before a full run; keep a sealed set from the start; change one thing at a time (one comparison broke this rule, see below).
What I Learned# The control decides the conclusion. The same model is “+27 points” against 0-shot and “no significant difference” against 4-shot. Data design matters more than training time. Training longer moved little. Many-option data and targeted synthetic data are what changed the results. Confirm the test set is sound before believing a score. Write down the experiments that did nothing. What Did Not Work# Distilling from Jev’s probabilities: no measurable difference from training on hard labels over the same 9,510 items. Jev agreed with the original labels on 73% of them, from 45% on JSTS to 95% on the synthetic items. A broader second batch of synthetic data (1,965 items across nine everyday scenarios): no measurable gain. Adding JCoLA training sentences (2,300): acceptability judgments stayed near chance. Training on public data alone made no measurable difference from 4-shot on unseen tasks. Trained to the end, the model is over-confident, and calibrated temperatures make out-of-distribution ECE worse. More on these and on what could come next: Taking It Further.
Mistakes I Made# Reported 95% on a test set without looking at its distribution. The 500 livedoor items were all from one category, so always answering that category scores 95%. With stratified sampling it is about 50%. Kept the old checkpoint rule in continued training. Selecting by validation loss on the old tasks stopped all three variants between steps 100 and 800, so most of the training went unused. The “pragmatics 63.3” I first reported was step 100. Trained to the end it is 69.3, at the cost of a more over-confident model. Changed three things at once. The second synthetic batch differed from the first in data, repetition count and the earlier items mixed in, so the two cannot be compared cleanly. Measured speed with memory full. The code computed vocabulary-sized logits for every position, which filled GPU memory and more than doubled the latencies. Let one author write both the training items and the test items. The gains on pragmatics and negation include some “same question style”. Also fixed along the way: a conclusion that “training broke double negation” came from 20 skewed items, and 100 minimal pairs showed the base model was weak there to begin with. The first validation set shared source texts with the training set, which made it optimistic until the splits were grouped.
If I Did It Again# Build the evaluation sets, the sealed set and the 4-shot control first, and check the test distributions, before the first training run. Have a person write the acceptance items, not the author of the training data. Run several random seeds from the start. In continued training, use the last checkpoint, or select on a validation set for the new task. Change strictly one thing at a time. Writing Synthetic Data# Decide what to fill first. It only helps where public data has nothing and the task needs it. Do not look at the test items while writing training items, and check for overlap by program afterward. Do not patch the test set’s errors. The training and test items should not share an author. This is the largest hole in this project. Control the answer distribution: cap the majority class, shuffle option positions, keep yes and no roughly even. Minimal pairs in groups (affirmative, negative and double negative differing in one place) help more than scattered items. Do not force a label on an item you are unsure about. Describe each level of a scale in words, and do not make the levels too fine. Keep the range broad, with several phrasings for the same question. A small synthetic set has to be repeated, but too many repetitions get memorized. Mix in earlier items so old tasks are not forgotten. Record the source and license. Fix the seed in the generator so it reproduces the same output, print statistics after generating, and read through the result. Accept with a control, change one thing at a time, and record it when nothing happens. Troubleshooting# Common failures of this recipe, collected while preparing and running it:
Symptom Cause Fix Loss stuck near ln(K), accuracy at chance The letter token does not match: training wrote " A" and the readout looks up "A", or the template has an extra newline at the end Use one render() for training and readout; encode the prompt plus " A" and check the last token id against the stored letter id Loss barely falls, but is not at ln(K) The prompt is not masked out of the loss, or the learning rate is too small (1e-5 is for full fine-tuning; LoRA wants 1e-4) Confirm the loss is completion-only; set 1e-4 CUDA out of memory on 8 GB Batch or sequence too long; model loaded in fp32; another program holds memory Batch 4 with gradient accumulation 2; shorten the maximum length to 384; confirm bf16; check nvidia-smi PyTorch on a Mac reports an unsupported MPS operator or a bf16 problem The MPS backend is incomplete Use MLX for both training and inference on a Mac; if PyTorch is unavoidable, enable the MPS fallback and use fp32 ModernBERT (the encoder route) slower than expected on a Mac Its speed depends on FlashAttention removing padding, which MPS lacks Run the encoder route on an NVIDIA GPU or Colab; on a Mac use the sdpa attention implementation and accept the slowdown ECE above 0.2 before calibration Normal. Small fine-tuned models are over-confident This is what fitting T is for. Fit it on the calibration set only, never on the test set ECE worse after quantizing a calibrated model 4-bit quantization changes the logit distribution Refit T after quantizing. 8-bit is nearly lossless; re-measure 4-bit The answer changes when options are reordered Option-order bias Shuffle the training data; add permutation consistency to the evaluation Test is good, a held-out source is much worse A normal out-of-distribution drop, or options without descriptions Add a one-line description to each option; mix more sources into training Irrelevant input is confidently assigned to a class Closed-set forcing, which Jev has too Add an other option with out-of-scope training items, and a separate yes/no gate. Both together are safest The Qwen3 base outputs <think> or a chat format An instruct model or a chat template is in use Use the Base model and plain text, with no chat template anywhere The same passage appears in training and test One passage has several questions Group by passage before splitting What went wrong on my machine:
Problem Cause Fix Loading a dataset fails with Dataset scripts are no longer supported datasets 4.x no longer runs script-based datasets Read the parquet branch on Hugging Face directly, only the needed config and split Training fails on the warmup_ratio argument transformers 5 removed it Use warmup_steps with a fraction between 0 and 1 An 8-hour overnight run trained only 1,913 steps The laptop went to sleep Power settings to never sleep and do nothing on lid close; keep the thread awake from PowerShell Training killed in the middle of the night A Windows update upgraded WSL Add resume from checkpoint; pause automatic updates uv sync takes 40 minutes A slow download route to PyPI A one-time cost. Keep the project on WSL’s own disk, not under /mnt/d A batch of 32 is tens of times slower than single items Vocabulary-sized logits for every position filled GPU memory Compute the last position only A 500-item test set scores 95% The test split was not shuffled when read from parquet, so all 500 items were one class Stratified sampling over the classes Limitations# All-hiragana input drops accuracy by 13 to 47 points. Ordinal (score) questions are the weakest type: 63% even on the training sources. It cannot do kinds of tasks it was not trained on. JCoLA is close to chance. Knowledge questions do not improve with this kind of training. At most 16 options per question, because the readout uses the letters A to P. One forward pass per question; Jev answers several questions against one state in a single request. Jev itself is clearly stronger on the same items: 16 points on commonsense, 20 on pragmatics and more than 30 on knowledge. Still open:
Several random seeds, the sealed set, and acceptance items written by a person. About 1% of items get a different answer in a batch than alone. Four source texts appear in both the test set and the sealed set. The 0.6B speed has not been re-measured after the memory fix, and the Mac training code has not been run on a real machine. Manshu LLM: A Character-Level Transformer Language Model Built from Scratch# #LLM; #Transformer; #PyTorch; #FastAPI
Every LLM component (embedding, GQA, RoPE, sliding window, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, LM head) implemented from scratch, with both local and HTTP inference services.
Repository: (not public yet; local project manshu_llm)
The flowchart below summarizes the main pipeline, “data preparation → training → inference/serving”, along with the data flow of the model’s forward pass.
graph TD A[Tiny Shakespeare] --> B[download_data] B --> C[tokenize_data] C --> D[train.npy val.npy vocab] D --> E[train.py] E --> F[checkpoints] F --> G[infer.py] F --> H[serve.py] H --> I["/generate"] H --> J["/health"] K[Input IDs] --> L[Token Embedding] L --> M[Transformer Block x N] M --> N[RMSNorm LM Head] N --> O[Logits] Project Overview# Manshu LLM (v0.1.0) is one of my flagship projects, with two core emphases: implementing every LLM component from scratch (embedding, GQA, RoPE, sliding-window attention, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, LM head, etc.) and providing a complete inference service (local scripts plus a FastAPI HTTP API with greedy/sampling decoding and health checks). The project covers the full pipeline of “data preparation → training → checkpoint management → inference service”, demonstrating a deep understanding of Transformers and LLM engineering. It uses character-level modeling, so no BPE or WordPiece is needed and the vocabulary is derived from the data. The default dataset is Tiny Shakespeare, which suits small-scale experiments and teaching.
Tech stack: a decoder-only Transformer in PyTorch featuring GQA (grouped-query attention), RoPE (rotary position embeddings), sliding-window attention, a SwiGLU FFN, and Pre-RMSNorm, aligned with mainstream architectures such as Llama. Training uses AdamW, cosine/linear learning-rate scheduling, and gradient accumulation, all configured through YAML (configs/model.yaml, train.yaml, data.yaml). Inference supports greedy decoding and temperature / top-k / top-p sampling. The service is built with FastAPI + Uvicorn, exposing POST /generate (text generation) and GET /health (health check), with API docs at /docs and /redoc. Docker deployment is supported (Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, and build.sh under docker/). Project layout: llm/ (model, data, training, inference, utils), scripts/ (download_data, tokenize_data, train, infer, check_model), configs/, data/ (raw, processed, vocab), checkpoints/, and serve.py at the root.
Highlights# Every LLM component built from scratch: no reliance on Hugging Face or other model libraries. Token embedding, GQA, RoPE, sliding-window attention, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, and the LM head are all hand-written, which builds a solid grasp of the math and implementation details while staying aligned with architectures like Llama. Complete inference service: local inference (infer.py, greedy/temperature/top-k/top-p sampling) and an HTTP inference service (FastAPI POST /generate, GET /health, Pydantic request/response models, CORS, Docker deployment) that can serve text generation directly. End-to-end pipeline: data preparation → training → checkpoint management → inference service; a single project demonstrates the full engineering path “from raw corpus to a callable text-generation service”. Reproducible and configurable: YAML separates model/training/data configs, and training and inference share the same keys and loading logic, making experiments easy to reproduce and hyperparameters easy to switch. Character-level simplicity: a small vocabulary and simple implementation allow fast validation of architecture and hyperparameters on small corpora like Tiny Shakespeare, ideal for teaching and for walking through in interviews. My Role and Contributions# I handled full-stack development of the model, training, inference, and serving, with a focus on:
Implementing the LLM components: built the decoder-only Transformer’s token embedding, GroupedQueryAttention, RoPE, sliding-window attention, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, and LM head from scratch, including weight initialization and options like tie_word_embeddings; every submodule is hand-written with no model-library dependencies. Providing the inference service: implemented local inference (infer.py + greedy_decode / sample_decode with temperature, top_k, top_p) and an HTTP inference service (FastAPI POST /generate, GET /health, Pydantic request/response models, model loading in lifespan, CORS, Docker deployment) offering text generation and health checks out of the box. Data and training: CharTokenizer, CharDataset, collate_fn; a Trainer (gradient accumulation, checkpoint management, validation), AdamW, learning-rate scheduling, and loss/optimizer wrappers. Category Technology Purpose Deep learning framework PyTorch Model implementation, training, and inference Model architecture Decoder-only Transformer Backbone of the character-level LM Attention GQA + RoPE + sliding window Grouped queries, positional encoding, long-context optimization FFN / normalization SwiGLU + RMSNorm Feed-forward network and Pre-Norm Training AdamW + Cosine/Linear LR + gradient accumulation Optimizer and learning-rate scheduling Configuration YAML (configs/) Model, training, and data configs API service FastAPI + Uvicorn Text generation and health checks Deployment Docker (optional) Containerized runtime Background# Implementing a language model from scratch builds a deep understanding of every part of a Transformer: embeddings, attention, positional encoding, FFN, loss, and sampling. Simply calling existing libraries makes it hard to master the details of GQA, RoPE, and sliding windows, or their impact on memory and long sequences. This project implements every LLM component from scratch and ties “model architecture → data pipeline → training loop → inference service (local + HTTP API)” into a single runnable, configurable codebase, making it easy to experiment with different layer counts, window sizes, and sampling strategies. It serves as a flagship project demonstrating deep understanding of Transformers and LLM engineering, highlighting the full-stack ability to “implement every component and ship an inference service” on a resume or portfolio.
Why character-level? Character-level modeling needs no BPE/WordPiece; the vocabulary is derived from the data and is small, so implementation and debugging are simple, and architecture and hyperparameters can be validated quickly on small corpora like Tiny Shakespeare. To move to subword tokenization later, only the tokenizer and vocabulary path need to change; the existing training and inference pipelines can be reused.
Choosing character-level over subword/word-level prioritizes interpretability and fast experiment iteration in this project. For larger corpora and stronger results, subword tokenization and larger configurations can be plugged into the same codebase.
System Architecture and Design Choices# The overall design is single-machine training with a single-process service.
Data flow: raw text (e.g., data/raw/tiny_shakespeare.txt) is read by tokenize_data.py → CharTokenizer.build_vocab(text) counts characters to build the vocabulary (<unk>=0 + characters sorted by frequency) → tokenizer.encode(text) produces a 1D array of token IDs → split into training/validation segments by val_ratio → saved as train.npy, val.npy (dtype int32), and char_vocab.json.
Training flow: CharDataset(data_path, tokenizer, context_window) slides a window over the 1D array; each sample is a contiguous slice of length context_window+1, with the first context_window tokens as input_ids and the last context_window as target_ids (targets are the inputs shifted right by one). collate_fn stacks equal-length samples into (batch_size, seq_len), padding with pad_token_id=0 if lengths differ. Before each batch enters the model, a causal mask (L, L) is built from seq_len; the forward pass yields logits (B, L, vocab_size), and the loss is CrossEntropyLoss(logits, target_ids) (with ignore_index=-1 support). Within the accumulation window only backward runs; once gradient_accumulation_steps is reached, gradient clipping, optimizer.step, and scheduler.step are executed. Every eval_steps the model is evaluated on the validation set and a best checkpoint is saved if validation loss improves; every save_steps a periodic checkpoint is saved, capped by save_total_limit.
Inference/serving flow: on startup, infer.py or serve reads the three YAML files via load_all_configs(config_dir), takes vocab_dir from the data config to locate char_vocab.json, and loads the CharTokenizer. It builds the Transformer from the model config (injecting vocab_size=tokenizer.vocab_size), then loads weights with load_model_only(model, checkpoint_path). At inference time the prompt is encoded (an empty prompt starts from [[0]], i.e., <unk>), greedy_decode or sample_decode is chosen based on temperature, and the output is decoded to text. The server performs this loading inside FastAPI’s lifespan, and incoming requests call the generation logic directly; results are currently returned all at once (non-streaming).
Design rationale: PyTorch makes it easy to implement each module from scratch and to do gradient checks and shape debugging. GQA reduces the number of KV heads, enabling longer sequences or larger batches at the same parameter count. RoPE encodes position into Q/K, removing the need for an explicit positional embedding table. Sliding windows limit the attention span, lowering memory and compute for long sequences. SwiGLU and RMSNorm are standard in modern LLMs and help convergence and numerical stability. FastAPI and Pydantic make it easy to define request/response models and auto-generate OpenAPI docs, simplifying integration and frontend hookup.
Architecture alignment: the attention and FFN design in this project (GQA, RoPE, sliding window, SwiGLU, RMSNorm) matches open-source LLMs such as Llama and Mistral, so the understanding gained here transfers to tuning and extending larger models and existing libraries (e.g., Hugging Face).
Key Design Rationale# GQA (grouped-query attention)
Multiple query heads share one set of key/value heads, preserving expressiveness while reducing the KV cache and compute. This allows larger batches or sequence lengths under limited memory and matches current open-source LLM practice. Configured via num_attention_heads and num_key_value_heads (num_heads must be divisible by num_kv_heads).
RoPE (rotary position embeddings)
Position is encoded as rotations of Q and K, so relative position is represented by angles. This supports extrapolation and longer contexts, needs no positional embedding table in the embedding layer, and is compatible with GQA and sliding windows. Configured via max_position_embeddings and rope_theta (default 10000.0); RoPE is built per head_dim inside each block and passed into the attention layer.
Sliding-window attention
Each position attends only to tokens within a local window, reducing attention complexity from quadratic in sequence length to a function of window size, which significantly cuts memory and compute for long-sequence training and inference. Implementation: compute QK^T to get scores, then call apply_sliding_window_mask. With sliding_window_overlap=True the window is symmetric (position i attends to [max(0, i-w/2), min(L, i+w/2+1)]); with False it is an asymmetric causal window ([max(0, i-w+1), i+1]). The window mask is ANDed with the causal lower-triangular mask, invisible positions in scores are set to -inf, then softmax is applied and multiplied by V.
SwiGLU + RMSNorm
SwiGLU strengthens the FFN via element-wise multiplication of a gate and an up-projection (gate_proj → SiLU, up_proj → element-wise multiply → down_proj). RMSNorm replaces LayerNorm to reduce compute and dependencies, and the Pre-Norm structure (norm before each sublayer, then residual) improves stability in deep networks, consistent with Llama and similar architectures.
YAML configs + unified loading
Model, training, and data parameters are separated into configs/model.yaml, train.yaml, and data.yaml, and loaded into a single dict (keys “model”, “train”, “data”) via load_all_configs(config_dir). Training, inference, and serving share the same paths and keys, making it easy to reproduce experiments and switch device, step counts, window size, and other hyperparameters.
Features# Health Checks# The service exposes GET /health for liveness probes and load balancing:
Response body (Pydantic model HealthResponse): status (healthy / model_not_loaded), model_loaded (boolean), device (e.g., cuda:0 or cpu), model_info (optional; includes num_layers, hidden_size, total_params, vocab_size) Startup: lifespan loads the config, tokenizer, model, and checkpoint in order; if any step fails an exception is raised and the service does not start Errors: if the model is not loaded at runtime, POST /generate returns 503 with detail “model not loaded” Data Preparation# download_data.py: downloads the Tiny Shakespeare raw text from Karpathy’s char-rnn repository, saves it to data/raw/tiny_shakespeare.txt, and prints the character count (URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/char-rnn/master/data/tinyshakespeare/input.txt). tokenize_data.py: reads val_ratio (default 0.1) from configs/data.yaml; reads the raw text; instantiates CharTokenizer() and calls build_vocab(text) (counts characters with Counter, <unk>=0, the rest sorted by frequency); saves the vocabulary to data/vocab/char_vocab.json; encode(text) produces the full list of token IDs; splits it proportionally into training/validation segments, converts them to int32 numpy arrays, and saves them as data/processed/train.npy and data/processed/val.npy. Input/output paths are hard-coded in the script, matching the “download first, then tokenize” workflow. CharTokenizer (llm/data/tokenizer.py): char_to_id, id_to_char, vocab_size; build_vocab(texts) builds the vocabulary from text; encode(text) looks up each character to produce an ID list, mapping unknown characters to <unk> (id 0); decode(ids) converts an ID list back to a string; save_vocab/load_vocab read and write JSON. The vocabulary JSON is a character-to-id mapping.
Outputs: train.npy, val.npy (1D int32 arrays) and char_vocab.json (character → id). Data statistics (character count, token count, train/validation split, vocabulary size) are printed at the end of tokenize_data.
Model Architecture# llm/model/transformer.py: the main model. Input input_ids (batch_size, seq_len) passes through TokenEmbedding to get (B, L, hidden_size), then N TransformerBlocks, a final RMSNorm, and finally the LM head (or the transposed shared embedding) to produce logits (B, L, vocab_size). Supports tie_word_embeddings: when True there is no separate lm_head and the output is F.linear(x, embedding.weight). llm/model/block.py: a single TransformerBlock. First attn_norm(x) → GQA (with RoPE, sliding_window, mask) → residual; then ffn_norm(x) → FFN (SwiGLU) → residual. Input and output shapes are both (B, L, hidden_size). llm/model/attention.py: GroupedQueryAttention (independent Q heads; shared K/V heads repeated to match the number of Q heads) and MultiHeadAttention. scaled_dot_product_attention computes scores, applies the sliding-window mask (if configured), then the causal/general mask, and multiplies the softmax by V. create_causal_mask(seq_len) returns a lower-triangular boolean mask; apply_sliding_window_mask(scores, window_size, seq_len, overlap) combines the window mask with the causal mask and writes it into scores. llm/model/ffn.py: SwiGLU: gate_proj(x) → SiLU, up_proj(x) → element-wise multiply → down_proj; output keeps the input hidden_size. llm/model/rope.py: RoPE built from head_dim, max_seq_len, and theta, applying rotary position encoding to Q and K. llm/model/norm.py: RMSNorm(dim, eps); forward computes x / sqrt(mean(x^2)+eps) * weight. llm/model/embedding.py: token embedding, vocab_size → hidden_size. Core features: Pre-Norm (RMSNorm before each sublayer), GQA, RoPE, sliding window (symmetric/asymmetric), SwiGLU, RMSNorm, and optional tying of word embeddings and LM head (tie_word_embeddings). Weight initialization can be enabled via llm.utils.init.apply_llm_init (init_weights and init_std in model.yaml).
Training Pipeline# scripts/train.py: loads the configs (model, train, data), builds CharDataset(train_path, tokenizer, context_window) and CharDataset(val_path, …), with DataLoaders using collate_fn (from llm.data.collate); instantiates the Transformer (with vocab_size injected into the config) and the Trainer; runs Trainer.train(). llm/training/trainer.py: train_step(batch): batch is (input_ids, target_ids), both shaped (batch_size, seq_len); creates a causal mask (seq_len, seq_len); logits = model(input_ids, mask=causal_mask); loss = criterion(logits, target_ids), divided by gradient_accumulation_steps before backward; when (global_step+1) % gradient_accumulation_steps == 0, runs gradient clipping (max_grad_norm, default 1.0), optimizer.step, zero_grad, and scheduler.step; global_step increments by 1 each step. evaluate(max_batches): runs a no-grad forward pass over val_loader and averages the loss. save_checkpoint(is_best): writes the file via utils.checkpoint.save_checkpoint; when is_best, names it best_model_step_.pt and deletes the old best; otherwise names it checkpoint_step_.pt and maintains a saved_checkpoints queue, deleting the oldest file when save_total_limit is exceeded. Training loop: iterates over num_epochs, running train_step per batch; every eval_steps runs evaluate and calls save_checkpoint(is_best=True) if validation loss beats best_val_loss; every save_steps, if no best was saved at that step, calls save_checkpoint(is_best=False); supports early termination via max_steps. llm/training/optim.py: AdamW (learning_rate, weight_decay, beta1, beta2, eps); learning-rate scheduler options cosine, linear, and constant, with warmup_steps. llm/training/loss.py: CrossEntropyLoss(logits, targets) flattens logits and targets and calls F.cross_entropy, with ignore_index support (default -1). CharDataset: __len__ = len(data) - context_window; __getitem__(idx) takes data[idx:idx+context_window+1], with the first context_window tokens as input_ids and the last context_window as target_ids (targets are inputs shifted right by one), returning two 1D LongTensors.
Checkpoints: best_model_step_.pt (best validation loss; only the latest is kept) and checkpoint_step_.pt (periodic; count limited by save_total_limit), both saved in checkpoint_dir from train.yaml (default checkpoints).
Inference and Sampling# llm/inference/generate.py: greedy_decode(model, input_ids, max_length, device, stop_token_ids): at each step, runs a forward pass on the current generated_ids, takes the argmax of logits[:, -1, :] as the next token, and appends it to the sequence; supports a stop_token_ids list, marking a sequence finished when hit and exiting early once all are finished. sample_decode(model, input_ids, max_length, temperature, top_k, top_p, device, stop_token_ids): with temperature=0 it calls greedy_decode directly; otherwise each step divides logits[:, -1, :] by temperature, optionally applies top_k (keep the k largest logits) and top_p (nucleus: sort by probability and cut positions whose cumulative probability exceeds p), then applies softmax and samples with multinomial; also supports stop_token_ids. The current implementation runs a forward pass over the whole sequence at each step and does not use a KV cache. scripts/infer.py: checkpoint, prompt, max_length, temperature, top_k, top_p, config_dir, device_str, and num_samples are configurable at the top of the script. It loads the config and vocabulary (vocab_dir from data_config, path vocab_dir/char_vocab.json), creates the model, and loads weights with load_model_only. A non-empty prompt is encoded and reshaped to (1, seq_len); an empty prompt uses input_ids = [[0]] ( as the start token). Greedy or sampling decoding is chosen by temperature; if num_samples>1, multiple samples are generated in a loop. After decoding, if there is a prompt and the generated text starts with it, the “full” and “new” parts are printed separately; otherwise the full text is printed, along with character and token counts. Sampling strategy: temperature=0 means greedy; temperature>0 means sampling, combined with top_k (0 disables) and top_p (0.0 disables) to balance diversity and coherence.
Text Generation API# serve.py: a FastAPI app whose lifespan loads the configs, CharTokenizer(vocab_path), Transformer(model_config), and load_model_only(model, checkpoint_path), storing the model and tokenizer as globals. CONFIG sets checkpoint_path, config_dir, vocab_path, device (cuda if available, else cpu), host (0.0.0.0), and port (8000). POST /generate: the request body is GenerateRequest (Pydantic): prompt (required, e.g. “First Citizen:\n”), max_length (default 100, ge=1, le=1000), temperature (default 0.8, ge=0, le=2), top_k (default 50, ge=0, le=200), top_p (default 0.9, ge=0, le=1), num_samples (default 1, ge=1, le=5). The response body is GenerateResponse: prompt, samples (a list, each with text and tokens), and model_info (checkpoint, device, total_params, num_layers, hidden_size). temperature=0 calls greedy_decode, otherwise sample_decode; the output is decoded with tokenizer.decode, packed into a list of GeneratedSample, and returned. CORS is configured (allow_origins=["*"]) for cross-origin frontend access. Results are currently returned all at once, not streamed. GET / returns a welcome message and the endpoint list (generate, health, docs, redoc). If the model is not loaded, /generate returns 503 with detail “model not loaded”; errors during generation return 500 with detail “generation failed: …”. Running and Deployment# Typical workflow: run download_data.py to download Tiny Shakespeare, then tokenize_data.py to produce train.npy, val.npy, and char_vocab.json; then run scripts/train.py to train, with checkpoints written to checkpoint_dir (default checkpoints/). After training, use scripts/infer.py for local inference, or start serve.py to expose POST /generate and GET /health. For Docker deployment, see the docker/ directory (Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, build.sh).
Quick start: after training, run python serve.py and open http://localhost:8000/docs to try POST /generate (text generation) and GET /health (health check) interactively; the root path GET / returns a welcome message and the endpoint list.
Helper Scripts and Configuration# scripts/check_model.py: inspects model structure or weights (e.g., parameter count, shapes) for debugging and alignment. configs/model.yaml: num_hidden_layers, hidden_size, num_attention_heads, num_key_value_heads, intermediate_size, max_position_embeddings, rope_theta, sliding_window, sliding_window_overlap, rms_norm_eps, tie_word_embeddings, init_weights, init_std, etc. configs/train.yaml: learning_rate, weight_decay, beta1, beta2, eps, lr_scheduler (cosine/linear/constant), warmup_steps, max_steps, batch_size, gradient_accumulation_steps, max_grad_norm, save_steps, eval_steps, save_total_limit, device, num_epochs, checkpoint_dir, use_amp, amp_dtype, etc. configs/data.yaml: processed_dir, vocab_dir, context_window, num_workers, pin_memory, val_ratio, etc. Technical Challenges and Solutions# During implementation, targeted designs addressed masking and causality, training stability and long sequences, and a unified entry point for inference and serving, enabling stable training on limited resources and a consistent external service interface.
Sliding-Window Attention and Causal Masking# Challenge: the mask must guarantee causality (each token sees only the past) while restricting attention to a local window, so it has to satisfy both the lower-triangular and window-boundary constraints and fit the Q/K/V shapes of RoPE and GQA. If window and causal masks are applied separately, ordering and broadcasting must be consistent to avoid missing or duplicate masking.
Solution: in scaled_dot_product_attention, first compute QK^T / sqrt(head_dim) to get scores (B, H, L, L). If sliding_window is configured, call apply_sliding_window_mask(scores, window_size, seq_len, overlap), which builds window_mask (symmetric window [i-w/2, i+w/2+1] when overlap=True, asymmetric [i-w+1, i+1] when False), ANDs it with the causal lower-triangular mask, and sets invisible positions in scores to -inf. If an external mask (e.g., a causal mask) is also passed, scores are masked_fill’ed according to its boolean values (False becomes -inf). This applies the window first, then causality, and an (L, L) mask is unsqueezed to (1, 1, L, L) to match the scores dimensions. Each block passes sliding_window and sliding_window_overlap from the config, and the attention layer uniformly uses GQA + RoPE + this masking logic.
Training Stability and Long Sequences# Challenge: deep Transformers and longer context_window values can cause unstable gradients or out-of-memory errors; large batches are infeasible on a single GPU, and the loss curve needs to be smooth.
Solution: Pre-RMSNorm plus gradient clipping (max_grad_norm, default 1.0), running clip_grad_norm_ before each optimizer.step. AdamW (with weight_decay) and a cosine learning-rate schedule with warmup_steps avoid an overly high early learning rate. gradient_accumulation_steps accumulates gradients over smaller per-step batches before updating, emulating a larger batch while keeping per-step memory under control. Sliding windows limit the attention span, allowing a larger context_window or batch_size within the same memory. The config optionally enables use_amp and amp_dtype (e.g., bfloat16) to further save memory and speed things up. The loss can use ignore_index (e.g., -1) for padding positions; in the current dataset equal-length samples are stacked directly by collate, so with no padding nothing needs to be ignored. If variable lengths are supported in the future, pad positions in target_ids can be filled with -1.
Unified Entry Point for Inference and Serving# Challenge: both infer.py and serve.py must load the same model and tokenizer, consistent with the config and vocabulary path used in training, to avoid scattered configs causing load failures or dimension mismatches (e.g., vocab_size or hidden_size inconsistent with the checkpoint).
Solution: both read the three YAML files via load_all_configs(config_dir), yielding model, train, and data sub-dicts. For the vocabulary path, infer takes vocab_dir from data_config and joins vocab_dir / "char_vocab.json", while serve’s CONFIG hard-codes vocab_path (e.g., data/vocab/char_vocab.json). Before constructing the model, model_config[“vocab_size”] is set to tokenizer.vocab_size and passed into Transformer(config), keeping it consistent with training (the training script likewise injects vocab_size from the tokenizer). The checkpoint path is configured separately in serve’s CONFIG and in the variables at the top of infer, and must match the training output filename (e.g., best_model.pt or best_model_step_*.pt). Training, inference, and serving thus share the same config keys and loading logic, differing only in the entry point (script variables vs. CONFIG).
Summary# As a flagship personal project, Manshu LLM highlights two things: first, implementing every LLM component from scratch (token embedding, GQA, RoPE, sliding-window attention, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, LM head, etc.) without relying on model libraries; second, providing a complete inference service (local infer.py plus FastAPI POST /generate and GET /health) with greedy/sampling decoding and health checks, ready to serve text generation. The project covers the full pipeline from data preparation, training, and checkpoint management to the inference service, with YAML configuration and Docker deployment options.
Future directions: add a KV cache to inference and the API to speed up long-sequence generation; support streaming responses (e.g., SSE); wrap the model and tokenizer in Hugging Face-style from_pretrained/save_pretrained; and add more datasets and evaluation metrics to compare architectures and hyperparameters.
